findings: The clearest candidate contrast is whether a concrete purchase/technical next step gets completed and the requirement set narrows enough for a decision. Director approval and contract movement appear in WON cases, but neither price acceptance, near-term intent, technical activity, nor customer samples alone separate outcomes. 18615 and 7601 are useful repeat-pipeline counterexamples: both involved extended technical work and alternatives, while only 18615 reached an explicit supplier preference and contract path.

candidate_features.feature_name: Explicit decision path with an owner and milestone
candidate_features.short_definition: The customer identifies who must approve or review the purchase, what that person or group will do, and a concrete expected decision or feedback point.
candidate_features.jev_question: Is the next purchase decision step tied to an identified customer role and an expected time or deliverable?
candidate_features.when_observable: After qualification, once the customer describes internal approval; classify only from statements made by the snapshot time.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Director is the decision maker; customer says they are leaning to this offer and expects to decide that day.
Contract is with the general director for review; customer says it is acceptable and plans to sign.
Only this supplier is under consideration at that point; customer will discuss with the director and report the purchase decision the next day.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: The customer has shown the offer to the mechanic but not yet to leadership; the leadership review is deferred.
Customer says procurement will contact the seller but cannot identify which of four buyers or provide a direct contact.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Customer calls himself the decision maker, yet the actual purchasing contact remains unnamed and the next step does not materialize.

possible_confounds: Manager worklogs summarize the customer process and may overstate certainty.
A short, one-person purchase can have a clear decision path without a named committee.
candidate_features.notes: The usable pattern is an observable process with a responsible role and a dated/actionable milestone, not a generic claim that the customer is the decision maker.

candidate_features.feature_name: Customer completes an agreed next step
candidate_features.short_definition: A mutually agreed customer action (visit, review, document, technical answer) occurs or is delivered by the stated checkpoint.
candidate_features.jev_question: By the current snapshot, has the customer completed the last specific next step they committed to?
candidate_features.when_observable: At each meaningful checkpoint after a customer commitment; distinguish not yet due from overdue.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Customer attended the agreed factory visit and completed a product run on the equipment.
Customer supplied visitor names and attended the previously arranged factory visit.
After the agreed offer review, customer returned the completed questionnaire and production approved the specified equipment.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Customer again moves the promised measurements to a later date; on Aug 5 the dimensions are still missing.
Customer asks to return to the proposal the following week; the Aug 25 discussion still has no actionable description of the rejected block.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Customer did ship physical product samples, but the evaluation exposed a two-machine configuration and the project did not progress to a purchase decision.
The customer rescheduled the planned factory visit before later attending; a single moved date should not count as a negative pattern.

possible_confounds: Different action difficulty: a sample shipment or multi-department review takes longer than a simple call.
Date-only worklogs limit day-level precision.
candidate_features.notes: Potentially strong if defined around the last customer-owned commitment and not raw follow-up counts.

candidate_features.feature_name: Technical inputs are usable for a specific solution
candidate_features.short_definition: The customer provides the measurements, samples, or other requirements needed to select a concrete configuration, rather than only a broad description or incomplete images.
candidate_features.jev_question: Are the customer-provided technical inputs sufficient to define the proposed configuration at this snapshot?
candidate_features.when_observable: During discovery and before a final technical proposal; use only requirements known by the snapshot.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Production approved the equipment after the customer sent the requested product details and the seller resolved open questions.
Customer sends a corrected questionnaire/file after the precise missing package height is identified.
Customer supplies container images and dimensions for the requested conveyor and printer configuration.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Seller explains that the received images lack container and cap dimensions, so production cannot provide a solution.
Customer resists sending measurements for a broad range of label sizes; the exact data required for a reliable quote remains unresolved.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Customer supplied physical samples, yet the samples revealed a scope/configuration mismatch and did not secure a purchase.
Customer quickly sends several images early in the process, but later declines the requested detailed size set.

possible_confounds: Product complexity and number of formats determine how much data is needed.
The worklog may conflate seller requests with actual customer-supplied artifacts.
candidate_features.notes: Define sufficiency against the chosen use case; count of files or samples is not itself a feature.

candidate_features.feature_name: Customer raises specific, actionable technical questions
candidate_features.short_definition: The customer names a concrete uncertainty or required change that the seller can answer or reflect in the offer.
candidate_features.jev_question: Has the customer raised a specific, answerable technical or commercial question and engaged in resolving it?
candidate_features.when_observable: During proposal review and technical scoping.

won_evidence.paraphrase: After a director review, the customer asks detailed questions about conveyor length and product separation.
Customer initiates a call to request adding a printer and two cartridges to the contract specification.
Customer asks whether the equipment supports larger caps and whether that capability is included in the configuration.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Customer says a block is unsuitable but cannot specify which block or the needed change.
Customer still cannot provide dimensions needed to resolve the equipment fit.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Customer sends detailed technical questions and requests printer and table changes, yet the solution remains unacceptable.

possible_confounds: Question frequency can reflect configuration complexity, not buying intent.
Manager summaries may selectively log questions.
candidate_features.notes: The candidate is specificity plus engagement in resolution, not merely the presence or count of questions.

candidate_features.short_definition: Customer independently reopens the discussion with a purchase-related question, requested change, or concrete next action.
candidate_features.jev_question: Has the customer initiated a substantive follow-up about the purchase since the last seller contact?
candidate_features.when_observable: Any time after initial qualification; exclude acknowledgements, missed-call notices, and file receipts.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Customer calls the seller and raises questions from the director meeting.
Customer calls to request a concrete contract-specification change.
Customer asks the seller to call after a missed call while the purchase decision is being discussed.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Customer requests a call with their engineer and shares the contact, but the project later stalls.
Customer responds to the initial request with product images, but does not sustain later technical follow-through.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Substantive customer initiative is present in a LOST case.

possible_confounds: Visibility depends on the completeness of message/call capture.
Customer role and deal complexity affect who initiates contact.
candidate_features.notes: Atomic and labelable, but this shard shows no clear direction; retain only as a validation lead if other shards corroborate.

candidate_features.feature_name: A live product-fit validation is completed
candidate_features.short_definition: Customer participates in a real equipment demonstration or test using the relevant product/container and receives an observable result.
candidate_features.jev_question: What is the most advanced completed product-fit check: none, samples sent, test/demo completed, or test accepted?
candidate_features.when_observable: After a test or visit has occurred and before a purchase decision.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Customer attended the factory and successfully ran the product on the equipment.
Customer and colleagues completed a factory visit described as successful; follow-up focused on final container changes.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Samples arrived for testing, but the proposed fit required a second machine and did not match the requested universal setup.
Seller invites the customer to inspect live equipment, but no visit is recorded in this shard.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Receipt of samples alone is not evidence that the customer accepted the test result or the configuration.

possible_confounds: Only two WON cases in this shard have a recorded in-person validation.
Higher complexity can make testing more necessary and correlate with longer deal cycles.
candidate_features.notes: Keep the stages separate: a planned visit or shipped samples are not a completed, accepted validation.

candidate_features.feature_name: The customer and seller converge on a bounded configuration
candidate_features.short_definition: The active use case and machine configuration narrow to a specific set of required formats/features that the customer accepts for evaluation.
candidate_features.jev_question: How bounded is the currently accepted configuration: unresolved broad range, narrowed with open exceptions, or explicitly accepted?
candidate_features.when_observable: After technical scoping and before commercial close; allow later changes if they are explicit and accepted.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Customer receives answers to its questions, a specific divider addition is priced, and payment terms are agreed.
Customer-requested printer and cartridge additions are incorporated into a revised contract specification.
Customer explicitly narrows the current project to equipment for the screw cap after other container variants remain unresolved.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Customer insists on one universal machine and rejects the two-machine alternative.
Customer explains that container sizes may change and the relevant format is still unclear.
Customer says the configuration is unsuitable but does not identify the block or define the required configuration.

counterexamples.paraphrase: This WON case also had substantial scope changes; convergence occurred later, so early instability alone should not be labeled negative.

possible_confounds: Product range and project complexity drive scope breadth.
A narrowed scope can be seller-imposed or omit real customer needs unless acceptance is explicit.
candidate_features.notes: Score the current accepted scope, not the raw number of requested formats or later implementation changes.

candidate_features.feature_name: Customer advances contract or procurement paperwork
candidate_features.short_definition: The customer reviews, edits, approves, or returns purchase paperwork rather than only receiving a seller-prepared offer.
candidate_features.jev_question: What is the customer-side document state: not started, under customer review, customer edits/approvals exchanged, or signed/returned?
candidate_features.when_observable: Only after a formal offer or draft agreement exists.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Customer obtains lawyer approval, requests a tax certificate, and the parties proceed to the electronic contract and invoice.
Customer returns a formal disagreement protocol for specific delivery clauses; revisions are later accepted.
Customer reports that the contract has been signed and is being scanned.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Offer is printed for internal review, but customer has not moved into contract paperwork.
Project remains at procurement-contact coordination and sample/testing discussion; no contract action is recorded.

counterexamples.paraphrase: Printing and discussing a proposal is not equivalent to customer-led contractual progress.

possible_confounds: This is late-stage and strongly correlated with deal progression; it may be a status marker rather than an early semantic feature.
Legal, funding, and e-signature procedures differ by customer.
candidate_features.notes: Jev-labelable, but low priority for early snapshots because paperwork is adjacent to outcome.

candidate_features.feature_name: Customer states a current preference after comparing alternatives
candidate_features.short_definition: The customer explicitly says which option they currently prefer and grounds the preference in an identified selection criterion.
candidate_features.jev_question: Has the customer stated a current preferred supplier or offer after comparison: none, several remain, this offer leads, or selected?
candidate_features.when_observable: After the customer has evaluated or discussed alternatives.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Customer says the director is considering only this supplier and will report the decision.
Customer says the project is currently considering only this company after prior comparisons.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Customer is still exploring other companies and has not decided whether a universal solution fits.

counterexamples.paraphrase: This eventual WON case spent weeks awaiting a China comparison and focusing on price; comparison activity itself is not negative.
A self-reported decision maker may still depend on an unidentified procurement group; a verbal preference needs a concrete basis.

possible_confounds: Seller worklogs may overstate customer preference.
A declared preference can be temporary and may precede technical fit or internal approval.
candidate_features.notes: Measure explicit customer-reported preference, not the presence or absence of competitors.

candidate_features.feature_name: Repeated postponement without new customer-owned evidence
candidate_features.short_definition: The customer repeatedly moves a promised decision or information step while no new artifact, accountable owner, or completed internal review appears.
candidate_features.jev_question: How many consecutive customer-owned milestones have been postponed without a new artifact or a named owner/date?
candidate_features.when_observable: Across repeated follow-up cycles before outcome; ignore one reschedule when the new commitment is completed.

won_evidence.paraphrase: Purchase is deferred while waiting for a supplier comparison and the product placement issue; customer gives a future checkpoint and remains technically engaged.
Customer moves the visit date but later completes the visit and test.

lost_evidence.paraphrase: Measurements are moved again, after prior promised dates; dimensions remain unavailable on Aug 5.
Customer postpones technical feedback to the next week; by Aug 25 the claimed mismatch is still not specified.

counterexamples.paraphrase: A WON project also had long waiting periods; it continued to produce customer-owned technical and management milestones.

possible_confounds: Long procurement cycles, travel, staff leave, or project urgency can create delays unrelated to intent.
Must distinguish a postponed but completed milestone from a repeated non-specific deferral.
candidate_features.notes: Atomic only if based on successive missed commitments and absence of new customer-owned evidence, not elapsed duration or contact counts.

standalone_rejections.reason: Appears in early worklogs for WON and LOST cases, including 18747 and 18775; not a standalone separator.
The same generic near-term wording appears in both outcome groups; 18615 and 7601 show that stated intent can coexist with extended or stalled processes.

standalone_rejections.pattern: Technical detail, photos, or samples by themselves
standalone_rejections.reason: Present in both groups; 7601 sent extensive samples and 18775 sent many images, yet scope or follow-through remained unresolved.

standalone_rejections.pattern: Number of calls/messages, duration, amount, source, pipeline, raw token volume, final stage/reason
standalone_rejections.reason: Explicitly excluded as standalone semantic features by task instructions.

risks: Only four deals per outcome in this shard; observations are hypotheses, not effect estimates.
Most manager_worklog records are date-only and marked year_inferred; pair the date with worklog_id and do not infer within-day order from these entries.

Some 18615 worklog entries predate its neutral.json created_at; this may reflect pre-opportunity history. Prefer post-creation evidence for snapshot studies and verify the timeline policy during synthesis.
Sales-manager summaries and call transcription may omit customer context or compress uncertainty.
Contract movement and expressed supplier preference can be outcome-adjacent; keep late-snapshot leakage risk explicit.
